question: ACAS is designed to keep aircraft clear of conflict:

options.text: Only when the ATC radar service has failed

explanation: ACAS gives an additional margin of safety by detecting and resolving conflicts independently of ATC. TCAS is the widely used alternative name.

question: To work, an ACAS-equipped aircraft must:

options.text: Carry a transponder and be able to interrogate others
Have the GPS position of every other aircraft nearby
Have a primary radar in the nose
Be in contact with ATC on VHF

explanation: The aircraft needs a transponder and the ability to interrogate other aircraft's transponders.

question: Which aeroplanes must carry at least ACAS II?

options.text: All aeroplanes flying under IFR, of any mass or size
Turbine aeroplanes over 5700 kg or with more than 19 seats

explanation: Turbine-powered commercial air transport aeroplanes of more than 5700 kg maximum take-off mass or more than 19 passenger seats must carry at least ACAS II (current software version 7.1).

question: On which principle does TCAS work?

options.text: ATC radar data passed by data link
Primary radar returns from other aircraft in its nose radar

explanation: TCAS interrogates the transponders of other aircraft and uses their replies to find range, bearing and, with altitude reporting, relative height.

question: Which inputs does a TCAS II computer use?

options.text: The flight plan from the FMS and nothing else
Mode S altitude, radio altitude, configuration and attitude

explanation: TCAS II uses pressure altitude from the Mode S transponder, radio altitude for its height-based inhibitions, aircraft configuration and performance limits, and heading and attitude from the IRS.

question: Where can TCAS traffic be displayed?

options.text: Only on the primary flight display's attitude sphere
On its own screen, the EFIS, the weather radar or the VSI
Only on a dedicated TCAS screen

explanation: Depending on the installation, traffic can be shown on a dedicated display, on the EFIS navigation display, on the weather radar screen or on an electronic VSI.

question: An intruder has only a Mode A transponder, with no altitude reporting. What can TCAS II give?

options.text: A traffic and a resolution advisory

explanation: Without the intruder's altitude TCAS cannot work out a vertical solution, so it can give only a TA.

question: An intruder reports altitude with Mode C. What can TCAS II give against it?

options.text: TAs and RAs in the vertical plane

explanation: With altitude data TCAS II can give TAs and vertical RAs. Coordination needs Mode S on both aircraft.

question: TCAS I provides:

options.text: Resolution advisories in the horizontal plane

explanation: TCAS I shows range, approximate bearing and, with Mode C, relative altitude, and gives "TRAFFIC, TRAFFIC" alerts. It gives no resolution advisories.

question: TCAS II resolution advisories give manoeuvring advice in:

options.text: Both planes, as turns and climbs

explanation: TCAS II RAs are vertical: climb, descend, increase or decrease climb or descent, monitor vertical speed.

question: When do two TCAS II aircraft coordinate their resolution advisories?

options.text: When both have Mode C transponders
When both have Mode S transponders
Whenever both are in radar contact

explanation: With Mode S data link on both aircraft the systems coordinate their RAs to give complementary vertical manoeuvres.

question: On which frequencies does TCAS II operate?
explanation: TCAS II uses the SSR principle air to air: it interrogates on 1030 MHz and receives replies on 1090 MHz.

question: Which aural message is a TCAS II traffic advisory?
explanation: A TA is "TRAFFIC, TRAFFIC". Climb, descend and monitor vertical speed are resolution advisories.

question: About how long before closest approach is a TA typically given?
explanation: Typically a TA comes about 20–48 s before the closest point of approach (around 40 s at higher levels) and an RA about 15–35 s (around 25 s).

question: About how long before closest approach is an RA typically given?
explanation: The RA threshold is typically 15–35 s, around 25 s at higher levels, so there is time to manoeuvre.

question: Close to the ground, which TCAS advisories are inhibited?

options.text: All RAs below about 1000 ft AGL
Climb RAs below 1500 ft above ground level

explanation: RAs are inhibited below about 1000 ft AGL (TA only); descend RAs below about 1100 ft and increase descent below about 1450 ft; TA voice messages below about 500 ft.

question: Below about what height is a "descend" RA inhibited?
explanation: Descend RAs are inhibited below about 1100 ft AGL, and increase descent RAs below about 1450 ft, to avoid driving the aircraft into the ground.

question: How is an aircraft generating a resolution advisory shown?
explanation: An RA intruder is a solid red square, a TA intruder a solid amber circle, proximate traffic a solid cyan diamond and other traffic a hollow cyan diamond.

question: How is an aircraft generating a traffic advisory shown?
explanation: TA traffic appears as a solid amber or yellow circle.

question: Proximate traffic is shown as:

options.text: A hollow cyan diamond, within 20 NM
A solid cyan diamond, within 6 NM and ±1200 ft
A solid red square, within 6 NM and ±1200 ft of height
A solid amber circle, within 6 NM

explanation: Proximate traffic is transponder traffic within 6 NM and ±1200 ft. It is not a threat and is shown for situational awareness.

question: "Other traffic" is shown as:

options.text: A solid cyan diamond with a tag

explanation: Other traffic is shown as hollow cyan diamonds within display range and normally ±2700 ft, extended to 8700 ft above or below with the above/below switch.

question: With ABOVE selected, other traffic is displayed within:
explanation: The above/below switch extends the display to +8700/−2700 ft (typically used in the climb) or +2700/−8700 ft (descent).

question: A traffic symbol has "+05" beside it and an up arrow. This means the intruder is:

options.text: 500 ft below and descending at 500 fpm or more
500 ft above and climbing at 500 fpm or more

explanation: The tag shows relative altitude in hundreds of feet, + for above and − for below. The arrow appears when its vertical rate is 500 fpm or more.

question: Beside a non-altitude-reporting intruder, the display shows:

options.text: A flashing question mark in place of the figure
No altitude number or trend arrow

explanation: An intruder with no altitude reporting has no altitude figure or trend arrow next to its symbol.

question: When TCAS tracks a TA or RA intruder outside the selected display range:

options.text: Half its symbol appears at the display edge
It is not shown at all
The display range changes automatically to show it in full
A full symbol flashes in the centre

explanation: An off-scale threat appears as half of its symbol, in its proper colour, at the correct bearing on the edge of the display, with its data tag if there is room.

question: TCAS cannot find an intruder's bearing. What happens?

options.text: Only a TA can be given
The intruder is shown straight ahead at the correct range
A no-bearing message shows; advisories are not degraded

explanation: A no-bearing message appears low in the centre of the display. TCAS's ability to compute TAs and RAs is not degraded by the lack of bearing.

question: A no-bearing message reads "TA 2.2 −04" with an up arrow. The intruder is:
explanation: It shows a TA at 2.2 NM, 400 ft below, climbing at 500 fpm or more.

question: With the TCAS function switch at ON:

options.text: The system is warming up but not working

explanation: STBY warms up the system; ON runs the transponder only, so others see you; TA gives traffic advisories only; TA/RA gives both.

question: When might TA ONLY be selected?

options.text: Always in the cruise, to reduce the crew's workload
After an engine failure, or on parallel runway operations

explanation: TA only is selected by specific procedure, for example after an engine failure when performance is reduced, or during parallel runway operations.

question: After a successful TCAS self-test, what is heard?
explanation: Pressing TEST runs a full built-in test; the voice says "TCAS SYSTEM TEST OK", or "TCAS SYSTEM TEST FAIL" if it fails.

question: Changing the TCAS display range from 20 NM to 5 NM:

options.text: Changes only the display, not detection or warnings
Reduces the interrogation power and so the detection range

explanation: The range selects 5, 10 or 20 NM for the display only. It does not alter the range at which aircraft are detected or advisories given.

question: What is a preventive resolution advisory?

options.text: An RA telling the pilot to avoid certain vertical speeds
A TA with a voice message
An RA that orders an immediate climb at 1500 fpm

explanation: A preventive RA, such as "MONITOR VERTICAL SPEED", restricts vertical speed without requiring a change. A corrective RA requires a change of vertical speed.

question: On an electronic VSI, how are RA vertical speed commands shown?

options.text: Amber for the speeds to avoid, white for the fly-to range
Red for the speeds to avoid, green for the fly-to range
Green for the speeds to avoid

explanation: The VSI shows red arcs over the prohibited vertical speeds and a green arc over the range to fly to.

question: On receiving a TA, the crew should:

options.text: Turn away from the traffic shown on the display
Search visually and prepare for an RA

explanation: A TA warns that an RA may follow. Look for the traffic, prepare to respond to an RA and ask ATC if concerned. Do not manoeuvre on a TA alone.

question: On receiving an RA, the pilot flying should:

options.text: Turn left to avoid the traffic
Look for the traffic before reacting
Wait for ATC to confirm it

explanation: Start the required manoeuvre at once, adjusting flight path, power and trim; the other crew look out; ATC is told as soon as possible of any deviation from the clearance.

question: Why must a manoeuvre never be made opposite to an RA?

options.text: The other aircraft may have been told the opposite
It would exceed the aircraft's performance limits
ATC will not know of the RA

explanation: The RA's sense may have been coordinated with the threat aircraft, which will be manoeuvring the other way. Opposing it could cause a collision.

question: When may an RA be disregarded?

options.text: When the traffic is visually identified and no deviation is needed
When ATC has given a different level to fly
When the aircraft is in cruise

explanation: Only when the pilots visually identify the conflicting traffic and decide no deviation is needed.

question: ATC instructs a descent while TCAS gives a climb RA. What should the pilot do?

options.text: Do whatever the other aircraft does

explanation: If an ATC instruction and an RA conflict, follow the TCAS advice.
